title: Czech culture and traditions
summary: Everyday customs at work and at home, the history behind them, all 13 public holidays and the traditions around Christmas and Easter, with phrases to practise.

phrases.en: Merry Christmas!
phrases.note: Vánoce is plural, so the adjective is plural too: veselé.

phrases.en: Happy holidays!
phrases.note: Common in cards and e-mails to colleagues in December.

phrases.en: Happy New Year!

phrases.cs: Veselé Vánoce a šťastný nový rok!
phrases.en: Merry Christmas and a happy New Year!

phrases.cs: Hodně zdraví a štěstí v novém roce!
phrases.en: Lots of health and happiness in the new year!
What did you get for Christmas? (lit. What did the baby Jesus bring you?)

phrases.cs: Na Štědrý den jíme kapra a bramborový salát.
phrases.en: On Christmas Eve we eat carp and potato salad.
Are you baking Christmas biscuits?
Happy New Year 2027 (on cards)
phrases.note: From French "pour féliciter". Seen on cards and in e-mail signatures in December and January.

phrases.en: Happy Easter!

phrases.cs: Hody, hody, doprovody, dejte vejce malovaný.
phrases.en: Hey, hey, give us a painted egg. (Easter Monday rhyme)
phrases.note: Traditional rhyme, in dialect form (malovaný for malované).

phrases.en: Where will you be for Easter?
phrases.note: o + locative plural: o Velikonocích, o Vánocích.

phrases.en: We're going to the witch-burning (30 April).
A kiss under a blossoming cherry tree! (1 May)
Happy birthday!
phrases.note: k + dative plural: narozeniny → k narozeninám.

phrases.en: Happy name day!
When is your name day?

phrases.cs: Dneska mám svátek, dejte si dort.
phrases.en: It's my name day today, have some cake.
Cheers!
phrases.note: Look each person in the eye as you clink glasses.

phrases.en: To you! (a toast to the person celebrating)

phrases.cs: Zítra je svátek, obchody jsou zavřené.
phrases.en: Tomorrow is a public holiday; the shops are closed.
We've got a long weekend.
Are you going to the cottage?
Where are you going for the long weekend?

phrases.cs: Ve čtvrtek je státní svátek, v pátek si beru volno.
phrases.en: Thursday is a public holiday; I'm taking Friday off.

practice.title: Christmas and New Year
practice.description: Wishes, customs and the grammar inside them.

exercises.prompt: Merry Christmas!
exercises.why: Veselé Vánoce! Vánoce is a plural word, so the adjective is plural: veselé.

exercises.prompt: Happy New Year!
exercises.why: Šťastný nový rok! (rok is masculine inanimate, so in the accusative of a wish it stays the same).

exercises.prompt: Přeju vám vesel___ Vánoce.
exercises.en: I wish you a merry Christmas.
exercises.why: Vánoce is plural, so adjectives describing it are plural: veselé Vánoce.

hints.explain: Vánoce is plural. Standard Czech is veselé (you will hear veselý in casual speech).
Vánoce is plural, not feminine singular: veselé Vánoce.

exercises.prompt: Co ti přinesl Ježíšek?
answers: What did {baby Jesus|the baby Jesus|Ježíšek|Jesus|little Jesus|the Christ Child|Santa|Father Christmas} bring you[?]
What did you get for Christmas[?]
exercises.why: In Czech homes, presents are brought by Ježíšek, the baby Jesus, on Christmas Eve.

exercises.prompt: What fish do most Czech families eat for Christmas Eve dinner? Type the Czech word.
exercises.why: kapr (carp), usually fried, with potato salad. Live carp are sold from tubs in the street before Christmas.

hints.explain: Right fish: now the Czech word, kapr.

exercises.prompt: What does **PF** stand for on a Czech New Year card?
exercises.why: PF = pour féliciter (French, "to congratulate"): PF 2027 means "Happy New Year 2027".

exercises.prompt: Wish her the same, and a happy New Year (you say vy to her).
answers: [{Děkuju|Děkuji|Díky}[,] ]{Vám {taky|také}|{Veselé|Krásné} Vánoce i vám}[,] a šťastný nový rok[!]
exercises.why: Vám taky (you too) or Veselé Vánoce i vám, then a šťastný nový rok.

hints.wrong: [{Děkuju|Děkuji|Díky}[,] ]{Tobě {taky|také}|{Veselé|Krásné} Vánoce i tobě}[,] a šťastný nový rok[!]
hints.explain: You say vy to her, so: vám taky, not tobě.

practice.title: Easter and spring
practice.description: Easter wishes and the spring customs.

exercises.prompt: Happy Easter!
exercises.why: Veselé Velikonoce! Velikonoce is plural, like Vánoce.

exercises.prompt: What is the braided willow whip used on Easter Monday called? Type the Czech word.
exercises.why: pomlázka: boys and men use it for a light, symbolic swat "for health and youth", and get painted eggs in return.

exercises.prompt: What are decorated Easter eggs called? Type the Czech word.
exercises.why: kraslice: decorated eggs, given to the boys who come round with the pomlázka.

exercises.prompt: What do Czechs "burn" on bonfires on the night of 30 April? Type the Czech word.
exercises.why: čarodějnice (witches): pálení čarodějnic, "the burning of the witches", usually a straw figure on the bonfire.

hints.explain: Right idea: now in Czech, čarodějnice.

exercises.prompt: O Velikonoc___ jedu domů.
exercises.why: o + locative. Velikonoce is plural, and the locative plural ends in -ích: o Velikonocích (at Easter), o Vánocích (at Christmas).

hints.explain: After o (at a time), use the locative plural: o Velikonocích.

exercises.prompt: O Vánoc___ jsme vždycky doma.
exercises.en: We're always at home at Christmas.
exercises.why: o + locative plural: o Vánocích (at Christmas).

hints.explain: After o (at a time), use the locative plural: o Vánocích.

practice.title: Name days, birthdays and toasts
practice.description: What to say when a colleague celebrates.

exercises.prompt: Happy birthday!
exercises.why: Všechno nejlepší k narozeninám: "all the best for (your) birthday". k + dative plural: narozeniny → k narozeninám.

hints.explain: k (for, towards) takes the dative: k narozeninám.

exercises.prompt: Happy name day!
exercises.why: Všechno nejlepší k svátku (or ke svátku). svátek means both "name day" and "public holiday".

hints.explain: k takes the dative: k svátku.

exercises.prompt: Cheers!
exercises.why: Na zdraví! (to health). Look each person in the eye as you clink glasses.

exercises.prompt: When is your name day? (informal)
exercises.why: Kdy máš svátek? (or jmeniny). svátek = name day.

exercises.prompt: On your birthday or name day at a Czech office, who usually brings the cake or snacks?
answers: the person whose {birthday|name day} it is
exercises.why: The person celebrating brings the treat (cake, biscuits, chlebíčky), and colleagues congratulate them.

hints.explain: In Czechia it's the other way round: the person celebrating brings the treat.

context.speaker: Kolegyně
context.cs: Dneska mám svátek, dejte si dort!
context.en: It's my name day today, have some cake!

exercises.prompt: Wish her a happy name day.
exercises.why: Všechno nejlepší k svátku!

hints.explain: It's her name day (svátek), not her birthday: Všechno nejlepší k svátku!

practice.title: Public holidays and history
practice.description: The dates your colleagues take off, and why.

exercises.prompt: Which date is the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution, now a public holiday?
exercises.why: 17 November: Struggle for Freedom and Democracy Day, remembering the student protests of 1939 and 1989.

hints.explain: 28 October is the founding of Czechoslovakia. The Velvet Revolution began on 17 November 1989.

exercises.prompt: Czechoslovakia was founded on 28 October of which year?
exercises.why: 28 October 1918, after the collapse of Austria-Hungary. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk became the first president.

hints.explain: 1993 is when Czechoslovakia split into Czechia and Slovakia. It was founded in 1918.

exercises.prompt: Which saint, the patron of the Czech lands, is remembered on 28 September?
exercises.why: 28 September is St Wenceslas (svatý Václav), now Czech Statehood Day. Wenceslas Square is named after him.

exercises.prompt: Which religious reformer, burned at the stake in 1415, is remembered on 6 July?
exercises.why: Jan Hus preached in Czech and challenged the Church; his death led to the Hussite wars.

exercises.prompt: Zítra je svátek, obchody jsou zavřené.
exercises.why: svátek here means a public holiday; zavřené = closed (plural, agreeing with obchody).

exercises.prompt: We've got a long weekend.
exercises.why: prodloužený víkend = "extended weekend". víkend is masculine inanimate, so the accusative is unchanged.

hints.explain: Understandable, but Czechs say prodloužený víkend (extended weekend).

exercises.prompt: The Munich Agreement of 1938 is often summed up in four Czech words meaning "about us, without us". Type them.
exercises.why: O nás bez nás: Czechoslovakia was not invited to the conference that gave its border regions to Nazi Germany.
